title: How Releasing Writers Completely Changed My Teaching
author: Olivia Eastwood
summary: Third-grade teacher Olivia Eastwood reflects on how adopting the Releasing Writers framework (formerly ThinkSRSD) transformed her writing instruction and her students' relationship with writing. Before Releasing Writers, her class used a different graphic organizer for every assignment, creating high cognitive load and constant student dependence; now one consistent framework serves all writing tasks across subjects, allowing students to internalize the process and transfer it independently. The shift from dependence to independence is the article's central theme: students who once raised their hands constantly now know their next steps from memory, own their work, and use models to push themselves rather than waiting for teacher direction. Eastwood also documents an affective transformation: writing had been both her and her students' least favorite time of day; after adopting the framework, students cheer when writing is announced. She argues that writing is the hardest synthesizing task students do—requiring simultaneous retrieval of spelling, organization, vocabulary, syntax, and ideas—and that a consistent framework reduces cognitive load enough to let students actually improve the quality of their thinking rather than just managing the process.
points: Switching from assignment-specific graphic organizers to one consistent Releasing Writers framework significantly reduced cognitive load and allowed students to transfer writing skills across subjects and contexts.

Student independence increased dramatically: rather than a constant stream of 'I don't know what to do next,' students now have internalized next steps and can navigate the framework from memory or notes.

Writing flipped from the least favorite to the most favorite subject for both teacher and students—a rare outcome that Eastwood attributes to students finally feeling ownership and efficacy over their work.
Releasing Writers includes self-scoring and goal-setting that forces students to independently improve their work each week, building metacognitive habits rather than reliance on teacher feedback.

Writing is the hardest synthesizing task students face—requiring simultaneous retrieval of spelling, organization, vocabulary, syntax, and ideas—and a consistent framework reduces enough cognitive load to let quality of thinking improve.
quotes: Before Releasing Writers: When we wrote, we used the curriculum organizers, which were different every single time. This meant learning a new system with every new writing assignment.

This change has significantly reduced the cognitive load on kids that usually comes with writing. This consistency also allows kids to translate the skills into any writing task, in any subject. Instead of each graphic organizer and process being specific to the prompt, they are general, so students are repeating the process over and over, internalizing the process and using them in any setting.

Before Releasing Writers: I used to hear: 'I don't know what to do next' or 'I'm stuck' all of the time. Writing can be one of the most cognitively challenging tasks for students. Between mechanics, syntax, idea production, organization, vocabulary, and the many other pieces involved in writing, when there is no consistent process or framework, students got even more overwhelmed.

Students cheer 'yes!' when I announce we are doing writing. Students who previously despised this time ask me every morning 'are we doing writing?', and it has quickly become my favorite subject to teach.
